newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanian BNR denies using reserves for oil imports.
newsitem.headline: Romanian BNR denies using reserves for oil imports.

text.p: Romania's central bank (BNR) denied on Thursday local media reports saying it had dipped into hard currency reserves to pay for vital crude oil imports.
Several newspapers this week quoted an executive from the state National Oil Company (CRP) as saying the central bank had spent $30 million for Romania's November crude oil imports.
"The BNR has not provided $30 million for any crude oil imports," central bank Vice-Governor Vlad Soare told Reuters.

"Such an operation is not possible because it would clash with stipulations in our international loan accords," he said in reference to credits given to the BNR by the international lenders over the past two years.

"Those credits were given to the BNR with the sole aim of consolidating Romania's hard currency reserves and not to finance energy imports," Soare said. "I want to make it clear that the BNR will observe all its obligations in the accords."

A shortage of funds put the CRP in difficulty with its payments for some 700,000 tonnes of crude imported over the past month. Half of that quantity has been blocked at the oil terminal in the Constanta port pending payment arrangements.
Disruptions to supplies of crude, following a legal dispute embroiling the CRP, have caused huge queues at petrol pumps across Romania and threatened the country's refining sector with closures.

The main oil trader Petrolexportimport SA says it made arrangements to open letters of credit with the state-run Bancorex SA foreign trade bank to guarantee payment for the crude. It also denied any BNR involvement in the operation.

"I confirm that the central bank is not paying for the crude. Today, we opened a letter of credit worth $22.5 million at Bancorex and will make arrangements for another $70 million," a Petrolexport executive told Reuters on Thurdsday.
The executive said the oil terminal had started to pump the crude to refineries, including 143,000 tonnes discharged by the tanker El Guardabia on Thursday.
The CRP's payment problems are related to a halt in talks with Chase Manhattan Corp on a $200 million credit.

Chase Manhattan asked the CRP to clarify its legal status after a local court ruling ordered the suspension of a government decree creating the CRP last July. A new hearing in the case is scheduled for December 2.

Court action to suspend the CRP was launched by a local private firm, which accused the state holding of monopolistic practices. The CRP has repeatedly denied the charges. -- Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264
